title: How to read a health headline
summary_es: Un estadístico explica por qué los titulares sobre salud se contradicen y qué tres preguntas hacerse antes de alarmarse.
prediction_prompt: Why do you think news stories about health so often seem to contradict each other?

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: Every week brings a new headline telling us that coffee will save us or kill us.

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: My guest, the statistician Sam Okoro, has spent years explaining why we shouldn't panic. Sam, welcome.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: Thanks, Nadia. And for the record, I had two coffees before coming here.

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: Brave man. So why do these stories contradict each other so often?

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: Mostly because a single study rarely proves anything, yet a single study makes a great headline.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: Science moves slowly, by accumulation. Journalism needs something new by six o'clock.

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: Give me an example of how a headline can mislead.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: Take the classic one: "Eating bacon increases your risk of cancer by twenty per cent."

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: Which sounds terrifying.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: It does, until you ask: twenty per cent of what?

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: Suppose that, out of a hundred people, five would develop the disease anyway.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: A twenty per cent increase takes that from five to six.

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: So one extra person in a hundred.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: Exactly. That's the absolute risk, and it's far less dramatic than the relative figure.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: Neither number is a lie, mind you. But only one of them sells newspapers.

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: What else should make us suspicious?

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: Size, for a start. A study of thirty volunteers tells you very little.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: And I'd always want to know whether the subjects were people or mice.

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: You'd be amazed how often that detail is left until the final paragraph.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: I wouldn't be amazed at all, sadly.

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: What about the difference between correlation and cause? Everyone's heard the phrase.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: Heard it, yes. Applying it is another matter.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: People who take vitamin tablets tend to be healthier. Is that because of the tablets?

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: Or is it that people who buy vitamins also exercise, sleep well and can afford decent food?

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: So the tablets might be a symptom of a healthy life rather than the cause of one.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: That's nicely put. Untangling those things is genuinely hard, and honest researchers admit as much.

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: Isn't there a danger that all this makes people cynical? That they stop believing anything?

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: That worries me more than the scary headlines, to be honest.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: Doubting everything is as lazy as believing everything. Neither requires any thought.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: What I'm arguing for is something in between: a kind of patient curiosity.

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: Which means what, in practice?

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: Asking three questions. How big was the study? Compared with what? And who paid for it?

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: The last one sounds a little cynical itself.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: It isn't an accusation. Plenty of research funded by industry is excellent.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: It's simply a reason to read the small print a bit more carefully.

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: Fair enough. I suppose we all prefer evidence that agrees with us.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: We do, and that's precisely when we should be at our most careful.

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: And if I haven't got time for small print?

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: Then wait. If a finding matters, it will still be true next month.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: The findings that vanish are usually the ones that were never solid in the first place.

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: So the best response to an alarming headline is to do nothing in a hurry.

segments.speaker: sam
segments.text: Precisely. Finish your coffee first.

segments.speaker: nadia
segments.text: Sam Okoro, thank you. That was reassuring, in a strange way.
